outfit: his usual mustard cardigan, white tee and olive trousers, plus a blue work apron and clear safety goggles pushed up on his forehead (his own red glasses stay on)
props: a small sketchbook he uses as a pointer
question: How did humans turn sand into clear glass?

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: You can't see through sand.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: So how are you looking through it right now?

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Your phone screen, your window, that glass of water.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: It's mostly melted sand.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: And the first glass people ever held?

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Nobody made it.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Take that yellow beetle in a young king's jewelry.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: It's glass, about 29 million years old.

graphic.big: How did humans turn sand into clear glass?

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: So how did humans turn sand into clear glass?

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: That beetle's glass most likely formed when a space rock hit the desert.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: People only had fire.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Along the way, there's a how-to guide in clay.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Step one: pick a lucky month.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: There's the world's favorite glass story, which its own writer passed on as a rumor.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: And there's one breath that made everyday glass cheap.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Each step adds a piece to this puzzle.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Fill it in, and you'll see the answer.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: So where did that beetle come from?

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: In 1922, Howard Carter found Tutankhamun's treasures.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: He listed the beetle as chalcedony, a kind of stone.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: In 1998, an Italian mineral expert, Vincenzo de Michele, took a closer look.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: It wasn't stone at all.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: This was desert glass, from western Egypt.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Chunks of it lie across thousands of square kilometers.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: It's canary yellow and nearly pure silica, the main stuff in sand.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: And it formed about 29 million years ago.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: In 2019, scientists found tiny minerals that only form in a huge impact.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: The best bet: a space rock hit the ground.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Nature made glass another way too: volcanoes.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Volcanic glass is called obsidian, and it's black and shiny.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: More than 8,000 years ago, people at Çatalhöyük, in today's Turkey, polished it into mirrors.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Some still give a sharp reflection.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Your bathroom mirror has a very old, very volcanic ancestor.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: But here's the catch.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: People could shape natural glass and polish it.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: They couldn't melt it, or make any more.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: First piece: NATURE.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: People knew glass long before they could make it.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: So who made the first glass by hand?

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Probably someone who was trying to make something else.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Nobody set out to invent glass.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: It probably started as a coating.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: About 6,000 years ago, craftspeople made something called faience.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: It's crushed quartz with a glassy skin, often bright blue.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: That skin was a glaze, a bit like the shine on your coffee mug.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: The Met museum calls it an early forerunner of glass.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Then, about 4,500 years ago, the oldest glass made by people shows up.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Small beads, most likely from Mesopotamia, around today's Iraq.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: How did people get there?

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Nobody knows for sure, but there are good guesses.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Maybe a glaze got so thick that it could stand on its own.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Or maybe it was a leftover from metalworking fires.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: The Getty Museum says it was possibly a very fortunate accident.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Piece two: ACCIDENT.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Glass most likely began as a side effect, not a plan.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: For about a thousand years, glass beads stayed rare.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Then kings got involved.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: And that's where the paperwork gets strange.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Egypt, about 3,350 years ago.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: A pharaoh sends word that he wants glass.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: The reply comes on a clay tablet, from a ruler on the eastern Mediterranean coast.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: His name is Yidya, and he's sending 30 pieces of glass.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Thirty pieces, for a king.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: That's how precious glass still was.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Egypt also made its own.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: One glass factory stood at Qantir, in the Nile Delta.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: In 2005, researchers Thilo Rehren and Edgar Pusch described how it worked.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: And one surprise: no sand.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Workers crushed quartz pebbles and heated them in old clay jars.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Then they colored the glass and cast it into round blocks.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Those blocks are called ingots, and they traveled far.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: About 3,300 years ago, a trading ship sank off today's Turkey, carrying blue glass blocks.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Tests show some of that glass was made in Egypt.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: It was probably on its way to ancient Greece.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: But how did people pass on the recipe?

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: They wrote it down, in clay.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: The best-known copies come from a royal library at Nineveh.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: They're about 2,700 years old, and the recipe inside is older.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: So what's step one?

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: When you build the glass furnace, pick a good day in a favorable month.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Step two: keep strangers out.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: My flat-pack shelf starts with: check all the screws.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: This one starts with a calendar.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Piece three: RECIPE.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Glass now had a written recipe, and kings asked for it by letter.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: But where did glass first come from?

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Rome had a story for that.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Here's the most famous glass story of all.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Pliny the Elder, a Roman writer, told it around AD 77.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Sailors carrying blocks of soda land on a sandy beach.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: With no rocks around, they rest their cooking pots on soda lumps.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: The fire roars.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Soon the soda mixes with the sand, and clear streams start to flow.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: The soda block, if it could talk: I was only holding up a pot!

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: But look at how Pliny starts: the story goes.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Even he wasn't sure.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Most experts doubt a beach cooking fire could do it.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Ancient glassmakers needed furnaces running hot for hours.

graphic.small: from the first glass beads to Pliny's story

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: And glass was already more than 2,000 years old when Pliny wrote.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Subscribe if you like myths checked like this — next up, how prehistoric humans told time.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Still, the story gets one thing right: soda.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Sand alone needs about 1,700 degrees Celsius to melt.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Ancient glass furnaces ran much cooler than that.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Add soda, and the mix starts to melt at around 1,000.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Chemists call soda a flux, a helper that makes things melt at lower heat.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: It was the ancient glassmaker's shortcut.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: So why is sand dull, but glass clear?

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Every grain of sand has edges.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Billions of edges bounce light around, so you can't see through a pile.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Melt the grains into one smooth piece, and the edges disappear.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Light goes straight through.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: So that's why a window is clear, and a beach isn't.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Piece four: SODA.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Before Pliny's time, glass was rare and slow to make.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: That was about to change, with one breath.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Until then, making a glass bottle was slow and fiddly.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Wind hot glass around a clay core on a rod.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Let it cool, then scrape the clay out.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: It worked, but only for small bottles like this one.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Then, a little over 2,000 years ago, someone on the eastern Mediterranean coast tried something new.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: This is the biggest leap in our story.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Imagine you're in that workshop.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: You dip a long, hollow pipe into a blob of hot glass.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Then you blow.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: The glass swells into a bubble, like chewing gum.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: In Jerusalem, archaeologists found the oldest blown glass we can date.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: It's workshop waste from about 50 to 40 BC.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Blowing was easier and cheaper, and it spread west to Italy.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: In Rome, says the Greek writer Strabo, a glass cup costs one copper coin.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: That's the Roman version of a one-dollar glass.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: More than a thousand years earlier, a pharaoh ordered glass by the piece.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Fancy glass could still cost a fortune.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Romans even put glass in some windows.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: But don't picture a modern window.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Roman panes were thick and greenish.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Some windows used thin slices of a clear mineral instead.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Piece five: BREATH.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: One breath turned glass from a royal gift into a cheap cup.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: But clear, flat glass was still far off.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: For that, we need an island.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Venice, 1291.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: The city's Great Council orders its glass furnaces out of town.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Their official reason: fire.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: So the furnaces moved to Murano, a small island nearby.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Secrecy came with it: glassmakers were banned from working abroad.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Today, a company just makes you sign a form.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: In the 1450s, Murano glassmaker Angelo Barovier cleaned up his recipe.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: He purified the burned plant ash he used as his soda.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: The glass came out so clear, Venetians named it after rock crystal: cristallo.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: But flat window glass was still hard to make.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Getting it truly smooth meant grinding and polishing.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: In 1952, in Britain, Alastair Pilkington started a strange experiment.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: He let hot liquid glass float on a bath of melted tin.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: It came out flat and smooth on both sides.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: No grinding, no polishing.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: His company announced it in 1959.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Today, about 500 float lines run around the world.

graphic.q: New glass made per person in 2014?

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Back in 2014, how much new glass did the world make per person?

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: About 2 kilos, 21, or 200?

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Take a guess.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: About 21 kilos each.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: That's like a heavy suitcase of new glass, for every person on Earth.

graphic.ans: Nature made it first. People learned the rest, one step at a time.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Piece six: CLEAR.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Venice made glass clearer, and a tin bath made it perfectly flat.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: So, how did humans turn sand into clear glass?

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Slowly.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Nature made it first, and craftspeople probably stumbled onto it.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Then, over 4,000 years, people learned to melt it, blow it and make it crystal clear.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: That yellow beetle needed a space rock.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: The glass in front of you took thousands of years of people trying.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: [pause] One more thing from Pliny.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: He heard a rumor about glass that could bend.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: But he called that story more widespread than certain.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: In 2012, a glass company showed glass you can bend.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: It's about as thin as a sheet of paper.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Sorry, Pliny.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Next: how prehistoric humans told time.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Subscribe so you don't miss it.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: And what's the oldest glass thing in your home?

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Tell me in the comments.
